prerequisites: Proper use of a scientific calculator.

learning_outcomes.text: Students should be able to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated through the development and defense of arguments and problem-solving within their field of study.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning, and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and aptitudes in the field of Industrial Engineering.
Ability to apply knowledge in practice.
Ability for autonomous learning.
Ability to manage information in solving problematic situations.
Students should be able to transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.

Ability to solve mathematical problems that may arise in engineering. Aptitude to apply knowledge on: linear algebra; geometry; differential geometry; differential and integral calculus; differential and partial differential equations; numerical methods; numerical algorithmics; statistics and optimization.
Students should be able to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include a reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects that enables them to learn new methods and theories, and provides them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems.
Ability to make decisions.
Ability for analysis and synthesis.
Ability for critical reasoning.
Competence in the critical contextualization of knowledge, establishing interrelations with social, economic, and environmental problems, both local and/or global.
Competence in the sustainable use of resources and in the prevention of negative impacts on the natural and social environment.
Competence in participating in community processes that promote sustainability.
Competence in the application of ethical principles related to the values of sustainability in personal and professional behavior.
Synthesize and descriptively analyze data sets.
Calculate probabilities in different contexts.
Identify real situations in which the most usual discrete and continuous probabilistic distributions appear.
Handle random variables and analyze their usefulness for modeling real phenomena.
Make decisions through the formulation of confidence intervals and/or hypothesis tests and/or linear regression techniques.

Use a statistical package to perform the following activities: synthesize and analyze data, perform simulations, calculate probabilities, hypothesis tests, linear regression problems, optimization problems.

syllabus_topics: 0. Set Theory and Combinatorics. Review of Set Theory. Review of Combinatorics.
1. Synthesis of statistical information. Unidimensional Descriptive Statistics. Bidimensional Descriptive Statistics.
2. Probability Calculation. Definitions. Conditional probability. Independence. Total probability theorem. Bayes' theorem.
3. Random variable. Probability distributions. Definitions. Discrete random variable. Continuous random variable. Discrete distributions. Continuous distributions.
4. Statistical Inference. Introduction to inference. Estimators, properties. Methods of obtaining estimators. Point estimation. Estimation by confidence intervals.
5. Hypothesis Testing. Parametric hypothesis tests for 1 and 2 populations. Non-parametric hypothesis tests.
6. Multiple linear regression. Simple linear regression. Parameter estimation. Model adequacy. Variable selection. Residual analysis. Estimation and prediction.
7. Introduction to linear optimization. Historical notes. Introduction to linear programming. Modeling optimization problems. Solving problems using the graphical method. Analysis of solutions.

9. Computer Lab Practices. Practice 1.- Treatment of Unidimensional Statistical Information. Practice 2.- Treatment of Bidimensional Statistical Information. Practice 3.- Probability. Simulation. Practice 4.- Probability distributions. Practice 5.- Central Limit Theorem. Practice 6.- Confidence intervals. Practice 7.- Parametric Hypothesis Tests. Practice 8.- Non-parametric Hypothesis Tests. Practice 9.- Multiple Linear Regression. Practice 10.- Introduction to Optimization.
teaching_methods: Lectures, exercises and problems using blackboard and audiovisuals, incorporating active methodologies and prior student work with virtual campus support.

Practical problem-solving sessions, seminars, and practical problems, fostering guided individual and group work with public exposition of results, supported by virtual campus and active methodologies.

Computer lab practices, solving problems and practical cases using software tools, with teacher guidance and supervision, individual or in small groups, supported by virtual campus and active methodologies.

Non-contact formative activities including independent student work to understand theoretical content, solve exercises and problems, develop computer practical cases, and conduct bibliographic searches.

assessment_methods.method: Tracking activities (computer practices, proficiency tests, glossary creation, problem-solving, active participation)
Progress tests (questionnaires with multiple choice, matching, short answer questions)
Completion of computer practical cases and control of computer practices (numerical resolution and interpretation of solutions)
Final exam (written and/or practical test including theory, theoretical-practical questions, and application problems)

assessment_rules: The final grade is based on tracking activities (5%), progress tests (5%), completion of computer practical cases (5%), and a final exam (85%). Errors in questionnaires will be penalized. For students who request global evaluation in due time and form, their assessment will consist of one or more theoretical-practical tests accounting for 100% of the final grade.
